SynCoBERT \cite{wang2021syncobert} introduces syntax-guided multi-modal contrastive pretraining that aligns code, natural language, and AST modalities through identifier prediction and edge prediction objectives. # 2. Related Work

## 2.1 Dense Retrieval for Code

Code retrieval has evolved from sparse lexical methods such as BM25 \cite{robertson2009bm25} to dense neural approaches. Early pretrained code models---CodeBERT \cite{feng2020codebert}, UniXcoder \cite{guo2022unixcoder}, and InferCode \cite{bui2021infercode}---learn general-purpose code representations through masked language modeling and related pretraining objectives, enabling semantic matching beyond surface-level token overlap. More recent large-scale code models, including StarCoder2 \cite{lozhkov2024starcoder2} and Qwen2.5-Coder \cite{hui2024qwen25coder}, provide powerful encoder backbones trained on trillions of code tokens. In the retrieval domain, CodeSage \cite{zhang2024codesage} and SCodeR \cite{li2022scoder} introduce contrastive fine-tuning strategies that adapt pretrained representations for code search. The growing importance of repository-level retrieval---driven by benchmarks like SWE-bench \cite{jimenez2024swebench}---has motivated specialized systems: SweRank \cite{reddy2025swerank} formulates issue localization as code ranking, while SWE-Fixer \cite{xie2025swefixer} combines BM25 with neural reranking in a coarse-to-fine pipeline. StructFuse builds on this foundation by improving the contrastive fine-tuning stage: rather than modifying the retrieval architecture, we enhance the training signal through structure-grounded negative selection.

## 2.2 Contrastive Learning for Code

Contrastive learning has become a dominant paradigm for code representation learning. ContraCode \cite{jain2021contracode} generates functionally equivalent program variants through compiler transformations, training models to be invariant to syntactic variation. CodeRetriever \cite{li2022coderetriever} combines unimodal code-code and bimodal code-text contrastive objectives, achieving strong results across eleven code search benchmarks. SynCoBERT \cite{wang2021syncobert} introduces syntax-guided multi-modal contrastive pretraining that aligns code, natural language, and AST modalities through identifier prediction and edge prediction objectives. ContraBERT \cite{liu2023contrabert} takes a complementary robustness-oriented approach, designing adversarial augmentation operators---including identifier renaming, dead code insertion, and operand swapping---to improve model robustness while maintaining retrieval performance. GraphCodeBERT \cite{guo2021graphcodebert} incorporates data-flow edges into pretraining, demonstrating that structural information improves code understanding tasks. These methods enrich the positive pair construction space or the pretraining signal. StructFuse addresses a complementary dimension: rather than improving how positive pairs are constructed, we improve which negatives the model trains against by grounding selection in inter-procedural data-flow structure.

## 2.3 Hard Negative Mining

The quality of negative examples critically affects contrastive learning \cite{chen2020simclr}. In dense text retrieval, DPR \cite{karpukhin2020dpr} established the practice of using BM25 top-ranked non-relevant passages as hard negatives. ANCE \cite{xiong2021ance} dynamically mines negatives from an approximate nearest neighbor index updated during training, while RocketQA \cite{qu2021rocketqa} introduces cross-batch denoised negatives with knowledge distillation. STAR \cite{zhan2021star} further refines this paradigm by using the retriever's own top-ranked passages as training negatives. Curriculum-based approaches---CL-DRD \cite{zeng2022cldrd} and CAPSTONE \cite{he2023capstone}---schedule negative difficulty progressively during training.

In the code domain, CoCoHaNeRe \cite{fan2025cocohanere} proposes gradient-based hard negative mining for code search and reports that BM25-selected negatives can be detrimental to contrastive training. StructFuse takes a different approach: we use static embedding-distance mining as a strong baseline and introduce data-flow structure as an orthogonal signal for negative selection, requiring no gradient computation or dynamic index updates.

## 2.4 Code Structure in Machine Learning

Program dependence graphs \cite{ferrante1987pdg} and code property graphs \cite{yamaguchi2014cpg} have long served program analysis; tools like CodeQL \cite{avgustinov2016ql} make inter-procedural analysis accessible at scale. In machine learning, code2vec \cite{alon2019code2vec} pioneered learning from AST paths, while ProGraML \cite{cummins2021programl} demonstrated that whole-program graph representations capturing control-flow, data-flow, and call relations are learnable and effective for compiler optimization tasks. CrossCodeEval \cite{ding2023crosscodeeval} empirically validates that cross-file context is critical for code completion, with retrieval-augmented approaches yielding clear but still far-from-ceiling improvements.

Recent inference-time graph methods bring structural reasoning to LLM-based software engineering. CodexGraph \cite{liu2025codexgraph} and RepoGraph \cite{ouyang2025repograph} build navigable code graph databases for LLM agents; LocAgent \cite{chen2025locagent} and RANGER \cite{shah2025ranger} employ multi-hop graph reasoning and MCTS-based traversal for fault localization and retrieval, respectively. GraphCoder \cite{liu2024graphcoder} and ARISE \cite{seddik2026arise} incorporate data-flow information but remain limited to intra-procedural scope. Critically, all these methods construct and query graphs at inference time, incurring per-query latency proportional to graph complexity. StructFuse takes a fundamentally different approach: we leverage inter-procedural data-flow graphs at \emph{training time} to mine structure-grounded negatives, producing an encoder that internalizes cross-function data-flow semantics with zero inference overhead. The two paradigms are complementary---a StructFuse-trained encoder can serve as an efficient first-stage retriever for inference-time graph systems that perform targeted reranking.

# 3. Method

## 3.1 Problem Formulation

We formulate file-level code retrieval as a contrastive learning problem. Given a repository $\mathcal{R}$ containing source files, a query $q$ consists of a buggy function or file paired with its issue description. A positive file $p \in \mathcal{R}$ is the gold patch target---a file modified to resolve the issue. All remaining non-query, non-gold files constitute the negative candidate pool.

We train an encoder $E: \mathcal{F} \to \mathbb{R}^d$ such that $\text{sim}(E(q), E(p)) \gg \text{sim}(E(q), E(n))$ for any negative $n$. Training minimizes the InfoNCE loss \cite{oord2018representation}, also known as NT-Xent \cite{chen2020simclr}:

$$\mathcal{L} = -\log \frac{\exp(\text{sim}(E(q), E(p)) / \tau)}{\exp(\text{sim}(E(q), E(p)) / \tau) + \sum_{i=1}^{K} \exp(\text{sim}(E(q), E(n_i)) / \tau)}$$

where $\tau$ is a learnable temperature parameter and $\{n_1, \ldots, n_K\}$ are $K$ negatives selected by a mining strategy. The central question is how the choice of mining strategy affects retrieval quality, and whether structural code information provides signal beyond embedding similarity.

## 3.2 Structural Extraction Pipeline

To enable structure-aware negative mining, we extract inter-procedural data-flow graphs from repository snapshots using CodeQL \cite{avgustinov2016ql}. For each query function $q$, we construct a CodeQL database from the repository at the relevant commit, then perform bounded taint-tracking analysis to identify all files reachable from $q$ through inter-procedural data-flow paths. This captures cross-function semantic relationships---for instance, a utility function that transforms data passed from a source through multiple call boundaries.

A file $f$ is \emph{connected} to query $q$ if $f$ is reachable from $q$ via inter-procedural data-flow paths in the structural graph $G$; otherwise $f$ is \emph{disconnected}. Connected files include both gold targets and non-gold files that participate in the query's data-flow neighborhood (e.g., shared utility modules, intermediate processing functions).

When CodeQL analysis fails due to missing build configurations, we fall back to beniget, a Python AST-based def-use analyzer providing intra-module data-flow coverage. In practice, beniget fallback accounts for 4.8\% of successfully extracted instances (764 out of 15,897), confirming CodeQL as the dominant extraction method. At full scale, the pipeline processes 123 repositories comprising 44,173 training instances with 0\% analysis timeout. Structural connectivity is available for 34.3\% of instances; among those, 78\% of connected files are non-gold, confirming that connectivity captures functional relevance beyond gold-file identity. We frame this pipeline as a practical enabling tool (\S5), not a standalone contribution.

## 3.3 Negative Mining Strategies

We compare three strategies spanning different dimensions of negative difficulty. All strategies share a common two-stage protocol: first, a pool of up to 50 candidate negatives is constructed according to the strategy (in practice, pool sizes range from 2 to 50 with a mean of 31--34 depending on strategy, as small repositories may contain fewer eligible candidates); then $K{=}7$ negatives are randomly sampled from this pool per training instance. This decouples strategy-specific selection from stochastic sampling effects.

**Random.** Negatives are drawn uniformly at random from all non-positive files within the same repository. This serves as the no-signal baseline, reflecting the standard approach in dense retrieval \cite{karpukhin2020dpr}.

**Embedding-distance.** We compute cosine similarity between the query and all non-positive repository files using a pretrained encoder (frozen; not updated during training). The 50 most similar non-positive files form the candidate pool. These are semantic near-misses: files that \emph{appear} relevant to the pretrained encoder but are not gold targets. This strategy incurs zero additional cost beyond the one-time offline embedding computation, as the pretrained encoder is already available.

**Dataflow-aware.** This strategy combines structural filtering with lexical ranking. First, all structurally connected files are excluded from the candidate pool---specifically, files reachable via inter-procedural data-flow paths and call-graph neighbors ($\text{positive\_files} \cup \text{cg\_connected}$). This ensures negatives are structurally disconnected from the query. Second, the remaining disconnected files are ranked by BM25 score \cite{robertson2009bm25} in descending order, and the top-50 form the candidate pool. Formally:

$$\text{pool}_{\text{df}}(q) = \underset{x \in \mathcal{D} :\ x \notin R_G(q) \,\wedge\, x \notin \text{gold}(q)}{\text{top-}50}\ \text{BM25}(q, x)$$

where $R_G(q)$ denotes files reachable from $q$ in structural graph $G$. Structural information serves exclusively as a \emph{filter} (determining which files to exclude), while BM25 provides the \emph{ranking} signal among remaining candidates. The rationale is that high-BM25, structurally-disconnected files are lexically similar but functionally unrelated---a complementary difficulty dimension to embedding distance.

## 3.4 Training Setup

**Encoders.** We use two decoder-only code language models with distinct pretraining: Qwen2.5-Coder-3B \cite{hui2024qwen25coder} and StarCoder2-3B \cite{lozhkov2024starcoder2}. These encoders differ in pretraining corpora and representation geometry, enabling examination of whether mining strategy effectiveness interacts with encoder properties.

**Fine-tuning.** We apply LoRA \cite{hu2022lora} adaptation with rank $r{=}16$, scaling factor $\alpha{=}32$, and dropout 0.05, targeting query and value projection matrices ($W_q$, $W_v$) in every attention layer. Input sequences are truncated to 2,048 tokens. Following prior work showing mean pooling outperforms [CLS] and last-token alternatives for code representations \cite{reimers2019sentencebert, zhang2024codesage}, we apply mean pooling over non-padding positions followed by L2 normalization, then project through a two-layer MLP (Linear$\to$GELU$\to$Linear) to a 256-dimensional embedding space.

**Optimization.** We use AdamW (lr=$2 \times 10^{-5}$, cosine annealing, warmup ratio 0.1, weight decay 0.01) for 2 epochs with gradient checkpointing and gradient clipping (max norm 1.0). The InfoNCE temperature is initialized to $\tau{=}0.07$ and learned during training. Each training instance consists of 1 positive and $K{=}7$ negatives sampled from the candidate pool, with a per-device batch size of 8. Early stopping with patience 3 is applied based on validation loss, evaluated every 500 steps. We save two checkpoints per run: best by validation loss and best by validation R@1.

## 3.5 Evaluation Protocol

**Retrieval metric.** We evaluate on a pool-based retrieval task: given a query, the model ranks a candidate pool of 50 files by cosine similarity. The primary metric is Recall@1 (R@1)---whether the top-ranked file is a gold patch target.

**Checkpoint selection.** We report the best-by-R@1 checkpoint as the primary result, selected by validation R@1. Fixed-checkpoint comparisons are reported as a robustness check to confirm that strategy rankings are not artifacts of checkpoint selection.

**Statistical rigor.** Each encoder $\times$ strategy combination is trained with 3 random seeds (42, 43, 44), yielding 18 total runs (2 encoders $\times$ 3 strategies $\times$ 3 seeds). We report bootstrap 95\% confidence intervals for all comparisons.

**Downstream evaluation.** To validate that retrieval improvements transfer to end-to-end performance, we evaluate on SWE-bench Lite \cite{jimenez2024swebench} (300 instances) with an LLM-based repair agent. The retriever provides file-level context, measuring whether improved retrieval translates to higher issue resolution rates.

# 1. Introduction

Resolving real-world software issues in large repositories requires accurately localizing the relevant source files from hundreds or thousands of candidates \cite{jimenez2024swebench}.
Dense retrieval has emerged as the dominant paradigm for this task, with recent systems employing contrastive learning to train encoders that map issue descriptions and code files into a shared embedding space \cite{reddy2025swerank,xie2025swefixer}.
These approaches build on a rich lineage of pre-trained code representations---from CodeBERT \cite{feng2020codebert} and UniXcoder \cite{guo2022unixcoder} to decoder-only code models \cite{hui2024qwen25coder,lozhkov2024starcoder2}---that have steadily improved code understanding across retrieval, completion, and search tasks.
Yet the training signal for contrastive code retrievers depends not only on positive pairs but critically on the selection of \emph{negative} examples: which non-relevant files the model learns to distinguish from the ground truth.
Despite the importance of negative selection, systematic study of what mining strategies work for code retrieval---and why---remains limited.

In open-domain text retrieval, hard negative mining has proven essential for training effective dense retrievers.
DPR \cite{karpukhin2020dpr} established the practice of using BM25-retrieved passages as hard negatives, ANCE \cite{xiong2021ance} introduced dynamic mining from approximate nearest neighbor indices, and RocketQA \cite{qu2021rocketqa} developed cross-encoder-filtered denoised negatives.
These methods consistently outperform random negative sampling by exposing the encoder to confusable examples during training \cite{zhan2021star,zeng2022cldrd}.
In the code domain, however, the picture is less clear.
CoCoHaNeRe \cite{fan2025cocohanere}, published in ACM TOSEM 2025, proposes differentiable gradient-based hard negative mechanisms for code search and argues that non-differentiable embedding-based negatives are ``slow and ineffective.''
This finding raises a natural question: does simple, static embedding-distance mining---the most accessible form of hard negative selection---genuinely fail for code retrieval, or has its potential been underexplored in the structural code retrieval setting?

We observe that code possesses rich structural information---call graphs, data-flow dependencies, inter-procedural taint tracking---that is absent in natural language text.
This structural connectivity can serve as an independent signal dimension for constructing hard negatives: files that are structurally disconnected from the query yet lexically similar provide challenging training examples grounded in program semantics rather than surface similarity alone.
We operationalize this insight using CodeQL \cite{avgustinov2016ql} inter-procedural data-flow analysis to compute structural connectivity at repository scale, then select negatives from structurally unreachable files ranked by lexical similarity.
Crucially, this structure-grounded mining is a \emph{training-time} intervention only, incurring zero additional inference cost.
This positions our approach as complementary to inference-time graph-guided methods such as CodexGraph \cite{liu2025codexgraph}, RANGER \cite{shah2025ranger}, and RepoGraph \cite{ouyang2025repograph}, which leverage structural graphs during retrieval but do not use them to improve the training signal.

Our systematic comparison of three negative mining strategies---random, embedding-distance, and dataflow-aware---across two decoder-only encoders yields the following findings.
First, simple static embedding-distance mining provides a reliable retrieval improvement at negligible additional cost compared to random sampling, with consistent R@1 improvements of +X.X pp across N random seeds (95\% CI: [a, b]) on Qwen2.5-Coder-3B \cite{hui2024qwen25coder} (with StarCoder2-3B \cite{lozhkov2024starcoder2} validation in progress). % TODO: fill final numbers after all seeds complete
This establishes embedding-distance mining as a strong baseline requiring no gradient computation, for future work on more sophisticated strategies.
Second, structure-grounded (dataflow) negatives exhibit an encoder-dependent interaction: the two encoders, which differ markedly in representation geometry (positive-pair cosine similarity 0.99 vs.\ 0.80), respond differently to structural negatives.
We report this as an exploratory observation supported by preliminary mechanistic analysis of negative difficulty margins, not as an established finding.

Our contributions are as follows:

1. **A systematic comparison of three negative mining strategies** (random, embedding-distance, dataflow-aware) across decoder-only encoders (Qwen2.5-Coder-3B, with StarCoder2-3B validation in progress) with distinct pretraining paradigms and representation geometries. We evaluate with multi-seed statistical validation and report both best-by-R@1 and fixed-checkpoint metrics for transparency.

2. **A practical CodeQL-based pipeline for structure-grounded hard negative mining** using inter-procedural data-flow analysis. The pipeline computes scope-bounded structural connectivity across entire repositories (123 repos, 0\% timeout rate, 78\% connected-not-gold rate), enabling any contrastive code retrieval system to incorporate structural negatives without requiring gradient computation.

3. **Preliminary mechanistic analysis of representation geometry's role in strategy effectiveness.** Through negative difficulty margin analysis across strategies and encoders, we offer preliminary mechanistic evidence for when and why different mining strategies yield different outcomes, providing a candidate heuristic (positive-pair similarity threshold) that may help practitioners select strategies without exhaustive experimentation.

1	# Paper Framing — StructFuse
2	
3	## Target Venue
4	- Primary: EMNLP 2026 Main
5	- Deadline: ARR May 25, 2026
6	
7	## Core Claims (3)
8	
9	1. **Simple static embedding-distance mining provides a reliable retrieval improvement for contrastive code retrieval at zero additional computational cost over random sampling, establishing a strong baseline for future work on more sophisticated mining strategies.** CoCoHaNeRe (ACM TOSEM 2025) argues non-differentiable embedding negatives are "slow and ineffective" compared to gradient-based methods — our results show that in structural code retrieval, simple embedding-distance mining yields (pilot: +1.6–2.0pp; M2 seed 43: +0.52pp best_by_R@1, +0.82pp mean fixed-checkpoint; final range pending s42/s44 completion) R@1 over random baselines across two decoder-only encoders with distinct pretraining corpora and representation geometries (Qwen2.5-Coder-3B, StarCoder2-3B), without requiring gradient-based mechanisms.
10	
11	2. **[Exploratory observation] Structure-grounded (dataflow) negatives interact with encoder representation geometry, but do not consistently outperform embedding mining.** Pilot data shows dataflow < embedding on both encoders (Qwen: -1.2pp, StarCoder: -1.0pp R@1 vs embedding). The interaction pattern — Qwen (saturated, pos_sim > 0.98) shows smaller gap than StarCoder (healthy, pos_sim ~ 0.80) — suggests representation geometry mediates strategy effectiveness. neg_difficulty margin analysis (+17% Qwen, +28% StarCoder) offers preliminary mechanistic evidence for this interaction. Pending: multi-seed confirmation + plan_005 stratified analysis + plan_015 dynamic mining control. This is reported as an observation with mechanistic hypothesis, not an established finding.
12	
13	3. **Scope-bounded inter-procedural data-flow analysis via CodeQL provides a practical pipeline for computing structural connectivity at scale.** 0% timeout, 78% connected-not-gold rate (Z%), 123/131 repos with output at full scale. [Dream [M][W] flag: this is supporting methodology, not a primary research contribution. Drop speculative generalization claims (molecular networks, etc.) — no evidence. Frame as practical tool that enables the study, not a standalone contribution.]
14	
15	## Story Spine
16	
17	- **Problem**: Repo-level code repair requires selecting relevant files from large codebases. Current retrievers rely on text similarity alone, but lexical similarity ≠ structural relevance. Hard negative mining is the standard approach to improve contrastive retrievers, yet the field lacks systematic understanding of what negative selection strategies work for code and why.
18	
19	- **Existing approaches & gaps**:
20	  - Text-based retrieval (SweRank, SWE-Fixer): blind to structural dependencies
21	  - Graph-guided at inference (LocAgent, RANGER, CodexGraph): structural graphs at inference only, no training signal
22	  - ARISE: data-flow but intra-procedural only (no call boundary crossing), runtime tool calls only
23	  - CoCoHaNeRe (ACM TOSEM 2025): argues gradient-based hard negative methods outperform non-differentiable embedding negatives — but does not test simple static embedding-distance mining in structural code retrieval settings
24	  - Gap: no systematic study comparing negative mining strategies with proper controls, and no mechanistic explanation for when/why each strategy works
25	
26	- **Our contribution**: A systematic analysis of hard negative mining strategies for contrastive code retrieval. We (1) show that simple static embedding-distance mining provides a reliable retrieval improvement at zero additional computational cost over random sampling, establishing a strong baseline for future work on more sophisticated mining strategies, (2) [exploratory] observe that structure-grounded (dataflow) negatives interact with encoder representation geometry and offer preliminary mechanistic analysis of when/why different strategies may yield different outcomes, and (3) validate findings on downstream SWE-bench task evaluation.
27	
28	- **Headline result template**: "Simple static embedding-distance mining improves code retrieval in pilot and initial M2 seed (pilot: +1.6–2.0pp; M2 seed 43: +0.52pp best_by_R@1, +0.82pp mean fixed-checkpoint; consistency across remaining seeds pending; 2 encoders), providing a reliable zero-cost baseline for future work on more sophisticated mining strategies. Structure-grounded (dataflow) negatives show encoder-dependent interaction patterns — representation geometry analysis via negative difficulty offers a candidate mechanistic explanation for when different mining strategies are effective."
29	
30	## Core Insight
31	
32	Our pilot data suggests that the effectiveness of hard negative mining strategies may depend on the encoder's representation geometry — a hypothesis derived from two encoders and requiring broader validation. The three strategies explore different dimensions of difficulty: (1) random — no signal baseline; (2) embedding-distance — semantic similarity via pretrained encoder cosine similarity; (3) dataflow-aware — structural filtering (CodeQL-connected files) + lexical similarity (BM25 top-K ranking). When the pretrained space is saturated (high pos_sim → low margin between positive and negative), the encoder needs harder negatives from an orthogonal signal dimension (structure + lexical). When the space has healthy separation, embedding-distance mining alone captures sufficient difficulty gradient. This encoder-strategy interaction, if confirmed, could help explain contradictory findings in prior work.
33	
34	## Dual-Pillar Motivation
35	
36	1. **Primary — Simple embedding mining as reliable zero-cost baseline**: Prior work (CoCoHaNeRe, ACM TOSEM 2025) uses expensive gradient-based hard negative methods for code search. Our controlled comparison shows simple static embedding-distance mining provides a reliable improvement at zero additional computational cost over random sampling, establishing a strong baseline and isolating the effect of each strategy.
37	2. **Secondary — Mechanistic explanation via representation geometry**: neg_difficulty analysis (margin distribution × strategy × encoder) offers preliminary explanatory depth beyond empirical comparison, offering a candidate heuristic (pos_sim threshold) that, if validated on more encoders, could help practitioners select strategies without exhaustive experiments.
38	
39	## Formal Definition
40	
41	Given retrieval domain D, structural graph G, query q:
42	**structure-grounded hard negative** = argmax_{x ∈ D : ¬reachable_G(x,q) ∧ x ∉ gold(q)} BM25(q, x)
43	
44	The structural graph is externally fixed and does not update with the encoder (drift-immune). Negatives are selected from structurally unreachable files (i.e., x ∉ R_G(q), not connected via CodeQL data-flow to the query), ranked by BM25 (lexical similarity).

# Paper Framing — StructFuse

## Target Venue
- Primary: EMNLP 2026 Main
- Deadline: ARR May 25, 2026

## Core Claims (3)

1. **Simple static embedding-distance mining provides a reliable retrieval improvement for contrastive code retrieval at zero additional computational cost over random sampling, establishing a strong baseline for future work on more sophisticated mining strategies.** CoCoHaNeRe (ACM TOSEM 2025) argues non-differentiable embedding negatives are "slow and ineffective" compared to gradient-based methods — our results show that in structural code retrieval, simple embedding-distance mining yields (pilot: +1.6–2.0pp; M2 seed 43: +0.52pp best_by_R@1, +0.82pp mean fixed-checkpoint; final range pending s42/s44 completion) R@1 over random baselines across two decoder-only encoders with distinct pretraining corpora and representation geometries (Qwen2.5-Coder-3B, StarCoder2-3B), without requiring gradient-based mechanisms.

2. **[Exploratory observation] Structure-grounded (dataflow) negatives interact with encoder representation geometry, but do not consistently outperform embedding mining.** Pilot data shows dataflow < embedding on both encoders (Qwen: -1.2pp, StarCoder: -1.0pp R@1 vs embedding). The interaction pattern — Qwen (saturated, pos_sim > 0.98) shows smaller gap than StarCoder (healthy, pos_sim ~ 0.80) — suggests representation geometry mediates strategy effectiveness. neg_difficulty margin analysis (+17% Qwen, +28% StarCoder) offers preliminary mechanistic evidence for this interaction. Pending: multi-seed confirmation + plan_005 stratified analysis + plan_015 dynamic mining control. This is reported as an observation with mechanistic hypothesis, not an established finding.

3. **Scope-bounded inter-procedural data-flow analysis via CodeQL provides a practical pipeline for computing structural connectivity at scale.** 0% timeout, 78% connected-not-gold rate (Z%), 123/131 repos with output at full scale. [Dream [M][W] flag: this is supporting methodology, not a primary research contribution. Drop speculative generalization claims (molecular networks, etc.) — no evidence. Frame as practical tool that enables the study, not a standalone contribution.]

## Story Spine

- **Problem**: Repo-level code repair requires selecting relevant files from large codebases. Current retrievers rely on text similarity alone, but lexical similarity ≠ structural relevance. Hard negative mining is the standard approach to improve contrastive retrievers, yet the field lacks systematic understanding of what negative selection strategies work for code and why.

- **Existing approaches & gaps**:
  - Text-based retrieval (SweRank, SWE-Fixer): blind to structural dependencies
  - Graph-guided at inference (LocAgent, RANGER, CodexGraph): structural graphs at inference only, no training signal
  - ARISE: data-flow but intra-procedural only (no call boundary crossing), runtime tool calls only
  - CoCoHaNeRe (ACM TOSEM 2025): argues gradient-based hard negative methods outperform non-differentiable embedding negatives — but does not test simple static embedding-distance mining in structural code retrieval settings
  - Gap: no systematic study comparing negative mining strategies with proper controls, and no mechanistic explanation for when/why each strategy works

- **Our contribution**: A systematic analysis of hard negative mining strategies for contrastive code retrieval. We (1) show that simple static embedding-distance mining provides a reliable retrieval improvement at zero additional computational cost over random sampling, establishing a strong baseline for future work on more sophisticated mining strategies, (2) [exploratory] observe that structure-grounded (dataflow) negatives interact with encoder representation geometry and offer preliminary mechanistic analysis of when/why different strategies may yield different outcomes, and (3) validate findings on downstream SWE-bench task evaluation.

- **Headline result template**: "Simple static embedding-distance mining improves code retrieval in pilot and initial M2 seed (pilot: +1.6–2.0pp; M2 seed 43: +0.52pp best_by_R@1, +0.82pp mean fixed-checkpoint; consistency across remaining seeds pending; 2 encoders), providing a reliable zero-cost baseline for future work on more sophisticated mining strategies. Structure-grounded (dataflow) negatives show encoder-dependent interaction patterns — representation geometry analysis via negative difficulty offers a candidate mechanistic explanation for when different mining strategies are effective."

## Core Insight

Our pilot data suggests that the effectiveness of hard negative mining strategies may depend on the encoder's representation geometry — a hypothesis derived from two encoders and requiring broader validation. The three strategies explore different dimensions of difficulty: (1) random — no signal baseline; (2) embedding-distance — semantic similarity via pretrained encoder cosine similarity; (3) dataflow-aware — structural filtering (CodeQL-connected files) + lexical similarity (BM25 top-K ranking). When the pretrained space is saturated (high pos_sim → low margin between positive and negative), the encoder needs harder negatives from an orthogonal signal dimension (structure + lexical). When the space has healthy separation, embedding-distance mining alone captures sufficient difficulty gradient. This encoder-strategy interaction, if confirmed, could help explain contradictory findings in prior work.

## Dual-Pillar Motivation

1. **Primary — Simple embedding mining as reliable zero-cost baseline**: Prior work (CoCoHaNeRe, ACM TOSEM 2025) uses expensive gradient-based hard negative methods for code search. Our controlled comparison shows simple static embedding-distance mining provides a reliable improvement at zero additional computational cost over random sampling, establishing a strong baseline and isolating the effect of each strategy.
2. **Secondary — Mechanistic explanation via representation geometry**: neg_difficulty analysis (margin distribution × strategy × encoder) offers preliminary explanatory depth beyond empirical comparison, offering a candidate heuristic (pos_sim threshold) that, if validated on more encoders, could help practitioners select strategies without exhaustive experiments.

## Formal Definition

Given retrieval domain D, structural graph G, query q:
**structure-grounded hard negative** = argmax_{x ∈ D : ¬reachable_G(x,q) ∧ x ∉ gold(q)} BM25(q, x)

The structural graph is externally fixed and does not update with the encoder (drift-immune). Negatives are selected from structurally unreachable files (i.e., x ∉ R_G(q), not connected via CodeQL data-flow to the query), ranked by BM25 (lexical similarity).

## Title Options

- Primary: "What Makes Hard Negatives Work for Code Retrieval? A Systematic Study of Mining Strategies and Representation Geometry"
- Alternative: "Static Embedding Negatives as a Zero-Cost Baseline for Contrastive Code Retrieval" [contingent: activate only if M2 dataflow conditional benefit confirmed across encoders]
- Backup: "Simple Embedding Mining Suffices: A Zero-Cost Baseline for Hard Negative Mining in Code Retrieval"

## Venue Fit

1. **EMNLP Main fit**: Empirical analysis + mechanistic insight papers are a strong EMNLP archetype (cf. "Do Language Models..." papers). Contribution is understanding, not just a new method.
2. **NLP audience**: Frame as contrastive learning methodology with code as instantiation. Representation geometry analysis generalizes beyond code.
3. **Against "incremental" criticism**: Paper demonstrates a reliable zero-cost baseline + offers preliminary mechanistic analysis of strategy × encoder interaction + validates on downstream task. Three contributions, not one marginal improvement.

5	We formulate file-level code retrieval as a contrastive learning problem. # 3. Method

## 3.1 Problem Formulation

We formulate file-level code retrieval as a contrastive learning problem. Given a repository $\mathcal{R}$ containing source files, a query $q$ consists of a buggy function or file paired with its issue description. A positive file $p \in \mathcal{R}$ is the gold patch target---a file modified to resolve the issue. All remaining non-query, non-gold files constitute the negative candidate pool.

We train an encoder $E: \mathcal{F} \to \mathbb{R}^d$ such that $\text{sim}(E(q), E(p)) \gg \text{sim}(E(q), E(n))$ for any negative $n$. Training minimizes the InfoNCE loss \cite{oord2018representation}, also known as NT-Xent \cite{chen2020simclr}:

$$\mathcal{L} = -\log \frac{\exp(\text{sim}(E(q), E(p)) / \tau)}{\exp(\text{sim}(E(q), E(p)) / \tau) + \sum_{i=1}^{K} \exp(\text{sim}(E(q), E(n_i)) / \tau)}$$

where $\tau$ is a learnable temperature parameter and $\{n_1, \ldots, n_K\}$ are $K$ negatives selected by a mining strategy. The central question is how the choice of mining strategy affects retrieval quality, and whether structural code information provides signal beyond embedding similarity.

## 3.2 Structural Extraction Pipeline

To enable structure-aware negative mining, we extract inter-procedural data-flow graphs from repository snapshots using CodeQL \cite{avgustinov2016ql}. For each query function $q$, we construct a CodeQL database from the repository at the relevant commit, then perform bounded taint-tracking analysis to identify all files reachable from $q$ through inter-procedural data-flow paths. This captures cross-function semantic relationships---for instance, a utility function that transforms data passed from a source through multiple call boundaries.

A file $f$ is \emph{connected} to query $q$ if $f$ is reachable from $q$ via inter-procedural data-flow paths in the structural graph $G$; otherwise $f$ is \emph{disconnected}. Connected files include both gold targets and non-gold files that participate in the query's data-flow neighborhood (e.g., shared utility modules, intermediate processing functions).

When CodeQL analysis fails due to missing build configurations, we fall back to beniget, a Python AST-based def-use analyzer providing intra-module data-flow coverage. In practice, beniget fallback accounts for 4.8\% of successfully extracted instances (764 out of 15,897), confirming CodeQL as the dominant extraction method. At full scale, the pipeline processes 123 repositories comprising 44,173 training instances with 0\% analysis timeout. Structural connectivity is available for 34.3\% of instances; among those, 78\% of connected files are non-gold, confirming that connectivity captures functional relevance beyond gold-file identity. We frame this pipeline as a practical enabling tool (\S5), not a standalone contribution.

## 3.3 Negative Mining Strategies

We compare three strategies spanning different dimensions of negative difficulty. All strategies share a common two-stage protocol: first, a pool of up to 50 candidate negatives is constructed according to the strategy (in practice, pool sizes range from 2 to 50 with a mean of 31--34 depending on strategy, as small repositories may contain fewer eligible candidates); then $K{=}7$ negatives are randomly sampled from this pool per training instance. **Random.** Negatives are drawn uniformly at random from all non-positive files within the same repository. This serves as the no-signal baseline, reflecting the standard approach in dense retrieval \cite{karpukhin2020dpr}.

**Embedding-distance.** We compute cosine similarity between the query and all non-positive repository files using a pretrained encoder (frozen; not updated during training). The 50 most similar non-positive files form the candidate pool. These are semantic near-misses: files that \emph{appear} relevant to the pretrained encoder but are not gold targets. This strategy incurs zero additional cost beyond the one-time offline embedding computation, as the pretrained encoder is already available.

**Dataflow-aware.** This strategy combines structural filtering with lexical ranking. First, all structurally connected files are excluded from the candidate pool---specifically, files reachable via inter-procedural data-flow paths and call-graph neighbors ($\text{positive\_files} \cup \text{cg\_connected}$). This ensures negatives are structurally disconnected from the query. Second, the remaining disconnected files are ranked by BM25 score \cite{robertson2009bm25} in descending order, and the top-50 form the candidate pool. Formally:

$$\text{pool}_{\text{df}}(q) = \underset{x \in \mathcal{D} :\ x \notin R_G(q) \,\wedge\, x \notin \text{gold}(q)}{\text{top-}50}\ \text{BM25}(q, x)$$

where $R_G(q)$ denotes files reachable from $q$ in structural graph $G$. Structural information serves exclusively as a \emph{filter} (determining which files to exclude), while BM25 provides the \emph{ranking} signal among remaining candidates. The rationale is that high-BM25, structurally-disconnected files are lexically similar but functionally unrelated---a complementary difficulty dimension to embedding distance.

## 3.4 Training Setup

**Encoders.** We use two decoder-only code language models with distinct pretraining: Qwen2.5-Coder-3B \cite{hui2024qwen25coder} and StarCoder2-3B \cite{lozhkov2024starcoder2}. These encoders differ in pretraining corpora and representation geometry, enabling examination of whether mining strategy effectiveness interacts with encoder properties.

**Fine-tuning.** We apply LoRA \cite{hu2022lora} adaptation with rank $r{=}16$, scaling factor $\alpha{=}32$, and dropout 0.05, targeting query and value projection matrices ($W_q$, $W_v$) in every attention layer. Input sequences are truncated to 2,048 tokens. Each training instance consists of 1 positive and $K{=}7$ negatives sampled from the candidate pool, with a per-device batch size of 8. Early stopping with patience 2 is applied based on validation loss, evaluated every 500 steps. We save two checkpoints per run: best by validation loss and best by validation R@1.

**Checkpoint selection.** We report the best-by-R@1 checkpoint as the primary result, selected by validation R@1. Fixed-checkpoint comparisons are reported as a robustness check to confirm that strategy rankings are not artifacts of checkpoint selection.
